newsitem.title: GERMANY: Easter in Germany is a time for...television.
newsitem.headline: Easter in Germany is a time for...television.

text.p: As German families gather for Easter and prepare to hunt coloured eggs, feast on huge meals and collapse in front of their televisions, experts are gearing up to see who will win a fierce ratings battle.

Competition among stations for weary eyes in what inevitably becomes a ratings bonanza -- more than 31 million viewers tune in of the country's 80 million people -- has become as much of a tradition here as the Easter Bunny.
Networks in Europe's largest television market pull the thoroughbreds out of their programming stables to win the war for viewers, the most important period next to Christmas.

This year's line-up looks to be no different with Hollywood blockbusters including "Schindler's List", "Dead Poet's Society" and "Maverick" going head to head on Good Friday and beloved German entertainers jousting for Easter Sunday viewers.
Then the tallying begins. Researchers at the Gesellschaft fuer Konsumforschung (GfK) ratings institute calculate raw viewer counts, prime-time winners and the draw among key demographic groups.
"The untrained eye can hardly tell the key differences between these figures," said a manager of a large German media agency, responsible for selling television advertising time.

But understanding the gulf between drawing more 14 to 49- year-olds between 5 and 8 p.m. versus capturing more of those under 50 who have a high school diploma is the bread and butter of the industry, media agencies say.
The GfK provides data from small meters which sit next to television sets in 5,200 German households. Data are collected overnight and sent to networks, agencies and investors over telephone lines.

The institute has built its reputation on a principle of strict neutrality and collects data exclusively based on a contract with the AGF Society for Television Research, which in turn represents seven of the top German networks.

With the introduction of demographic data linked to ratings, the GfK opened up new possibilities. Broadcasters and agencies can now poll specific viewers to create programming custom-made for certain target groups.

"The flexibility is practically limitless," GfK Director Darkow said, for media agencies and networks that invest in market research. He added viewer demographic data has become the most important instrument in planning programming.
But this added dimension often leaves determining what is a ratings coup or flop during the feverish spring period to the eye of the beholder.
Darkow said the swelling importance of viewer data in the industry was becoming almost immeasurable, and with it the hunt to crown oneself king of the television ratings.
"There are no false data," said Darkow. "But methods are applied in their interpretation, which is not our job, that sometimes skirt the border of the reasonable."
However, he added, "Everybody has the same access to information and most follow the rules."
Media agencies, responsible for millions of marks (dollars) in television advertising accounts and network time slots, often have the most to lose by such data "massaging".

"We don't allow ourselves to get irritated by it," said a representative of a Duesseldorf media agency, but he added that companies that make their marketing decisions purely "from the gut" could be more easily influenced by rose-coloured ratings.
